title: The Secret Sauce Behind NoSQL_ LSM Tree

segments.text: No SQL databases like Cassandra have exploded in popularity in recent years.
One driver is the insatiable demand to ingest huge amounts of data from an ever-growing
number of sources like mobile application and IoT devices.
The secret sauce behind many of these no SQL databases is a data structure called
log structure merge tree.
An LSM tree is optimized for fast rights.
To understand how an LSM tree works, let's first take a look at how data is typically
stored in a relational database.
A relational database is commonly backed by a data structure called B tree.
A B tree is optimized for reads.
Updating the B tree is relatively expensive, as it involves random IO and might include
updating multiple pages on disk.
This limits how fast a B tree can ingest data.
An LSM tree works differently.
Rights are bashed in memory as they arrive in a structure called a MAMM table.
A MAMM table is ordered by object key and is usually implemented as they balance binary
tree.
As a MAMM table reaches a certain size, it is flushed to disk as an immutable sorted
string table.
An SS table stores the key value pairs in a sort of sequence.
These rights are all sequential IO, they are fast on any storage media.
The new SS table becomes the most recent segment of the LSM tree.
As more data comes in, more and more of these immutable SS tables are created and added
to the LSM tree with each one representing a small chronological subset of the incoming changes.
Since SS tables are immutable, an update to an existing object key does not override
an existing table.
Instead, a new entry is added to the most recent SS table, which supersedes any entries
in the OSS tables for the object key.
Deleting an object requires special handling too, since we cannot mark anything in the SS
table as deleted.
To perform a delete, it is a marker called a tombstone to the most recent SS table for
the object key.
When we encountered a tombstone on read, we know the object has been deleted.
And yes, it is a bit unintuitive that a delete take up extra space.
To survey read request, we first tried to find a key in the MAMM table, then in the most recent
SS table in the LSM tree, then the next SS table and so on.
Since an SS table is sorted, the lookup can be done efficiently.
The accumulation of SS tables presents two issues.
As the number of SS tables grows, it will take an increasingly long time to look up
a key.
And as the SS table accumulate, they are more and more outdated entries as keys are updated
and tombstones are added.
These take up precious space.
To fix these issues, there is a periodic merging and compaction process running in the
background, to merge SS tables and discard outdated or delete a values.
This reclaimed this space and caps the number of SS tables a read has to look through.
Since SS tables are sorted, this merging and compaction process is simple and efficient.
The approach is similar to the one used in the merge phase of the merge sort algorithm.
This, in a nutshell, is how an LSM tree provides fast writes.
Let's recap.
An LSM tree buffers incoming writes in memory.
When the buffer fills up, we sort and flush it to disk as an immutable SS table.
The number of SS tables increases as more buffers get flushed to disk.
This creates a problem for reads as each read has to search through these SS tables
to perform a lookup.
To cap the number of SS tables it has to search through for each read.
The LSM tree merges the SS tables and compacts them in the background.
Let's look at the compaction process more closely.
When SS tables are merged, they are organized into levels.
This is where the tree part of the LSM trees come into the picture.
The different strategies to determine when and how the SS tables are merged and compacted.
There are two broad strategies.
Size tier compaction and leveled compaction.
Size tier compaction is optimized for right throughput.
Level compaction is more read optimized.
We won't go into too much detail on how these compaction strategies work.
They are a few key points to remember though.
Compaction keeps the number of SS tables manageable.
The SS tables are organized into levels.
With each level gets exponentially larger,
as SS tables from the level above are merged into it.
Compaction consumes a lot of I.O.
A missed tuned compaction could start the system and slow down both read and write.
Finally, let's visit some common optimizations for the LSM trees in production systems.
There are many optimizations strategies that try to provide read performance closer to that of the B tree.
What we explain below are just the common ones and they are by no means excessive.
To look up a key, it performs searches on the SS tables at every level.
Even though search is fast on sorted data, going through all the on this SS tables consumes
a lot of I.O.
Many systems keep a summary table in memory that contains the mean max range of each
this block of every level.
It allows the system to skip searches on those this blocks where the key does not fall within the range.
This saves a lot of random I.O.
Another issue that could be potentially expensive is to look up a key that does not exist.
This would require looking through all the eligible blocks at all the levels.
Most systems keep a bloom filter at each level.
A bloom filter is a space-efficient data structure that returns a firm no
if a key does not exist or a probably yes, if a key might exist.
This allows the system to skip the level entirely if the key does not exist there,
which dramatically reduces the number of random I.O. required.
In conclusion, no single databases backed by an LSM tree could be tuned to support a very high rate.
As with any database, proper tuning is the key.
For an LSM tree, Compaction Tuning is the most critical.
You would like to learn more about system design, check out our books and weekly newsletter.
Please subscribe if you learned something new.
Thank you so much and we'll see you next time.
